steps.say: The classic story is pain that makes no sense against a soft belly. A patient with atrial fibrillation suddenly develops severe central pain, yet the abdomen stays soft to press. Lactate climbs while the X-ray looks normal. That mismatch is an embolus until proven otherwise, and every hour of delay pushes mortality toward 90 percent.
steps.tx: Clot from **atrial fibrillation** (irregular heart rhythm shedding emboli) lodging as an embolus in the **superior mesenteric artery** (midgut vessel) gives **pain out of proportion** (agony with a soft belly) plus rising lactate, and delay carries **50 to 90** percent mortality. Emergency **embolectomy** (clot extraction with viability check) is the rescue operation.

vis.alt: Illustration of superior mesenteric artery embolus causing small bowel mucosal necrosis.
vis.caption: SMA embolus starves the midgut while the belly stays deceptively soft. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Do not open the belly before the scan in suspected mesenteric ischaemia. Biphasic CT angiography is the scan that finds the cutoff in the artery, gas in the bowel wall and gas in the portal vein. Those three findings plan the operation, telling the surgeon whether to pull clot or bypass. A lactate above 2 with a cutoff is an order for immediate theatre.
steps.tx: Biphasic **CT angiography** (arterial and venous phase contrast scan) is the test of choice, showing SMA cutoff, pneumatosis (gas in the bowel wall) and **portal venous gas** (gas tracking to the liver). Imaging precedes laparotomy to plan **embolectomy** (clot extraction) against bypass, since blind exploration wastes ischaemic time.

steps.say: Not every ischaemic bowel needs an operation. In intensive care patients on high dose pressors, the gut can shut down from low flow alone with all vessels open. The treatment is medical, with fluids, stopping the constricting drugs and prostaglandin to open the microcirculation. Operating on these patients adds a wound without fixing the cause.
steps.tx: ICU gut failure without clot is **nonocclusive ischaemia** (ischaemia from hypoperfusion, vessels open), driven by a pressor-dependent **low-flow state** (circulation too weak to feed the gut). Fluids, pressor weaning and prostaglandin drips reverse it, and the knife stays sheathed unless peritonitis declares itself.

steps.say: Clots in the mesenteric veins behave the opposite way to arterial emboli. These patients are sick but the bowel is usually alive, because collaterals keep it going. Blood thinners are the whole treatment, starting with heparin and continuing for six months. Surgery enters only when the bowel has infarcted or the belly shows peritonitis.
steps.tx: Venous-side clots define **mesenteric venous thrombosis** (thrombosed draining veins in prothrombotic or portal-hypertensive patients), treated first with heparin and then **6** months of **anticoagulation** (thinners). Bowel death or peritonitis alone forces resection; recovering patients switch to warfarin or a direct oral agent with clotting workup.

steps.say: No surgeon trusts a single look at ischaemic bowel, because the border between living and dead shifts over hours. The abdomen is left ready for a planned return at 24 to 48 hours. At the second look, dye or Doppler flow separates bowel that has recovered from segments that must now come out.
steps.tx: **Second-look laparotomy** (planned re-exploration) at **24 to 48** hours reassesses viability after **embolectomy**, using fluorescein dye or Doppler to separate viable from gangrenous segments. Marginal bowel is left in place at the first operation, since resection of stunned but living gut creates short bowel needlessly.

Bowel viable on dye or Doppler

steps.say: Months of fear of food with steady weight loss points to chronic bowel angina. Two of the three gut arteries are usually narrowed by atheroma, and eating hurts because the gut cannot pay the oxygen bill. Stents through the groin now fix most cases, with open bypass kept for failed or unsuitable anatomy.
steps.tx: Long-standing gut angina means chronic ischaemia: **food fear** (dreading meals for the pain that follows) with wasting, caused by **2 of 3** diseased mesenteric vessels. **Mesenteric stenting** (groin-access stents in celiac and SMA) fixes most, with open bypass reserved for failures; duplex watches for restenosis.

steps.say: A young thin woman with pain after every meal and every test normal may have a ligament pressing on her coeliac artery. The clue is pain that worsens when she breathes out, because expiration tightens the compressing band, easing again on breathing in. The kink is clear on duplex. Keyhole division of the ligament with nerve clearance is curative.
steps.tx: Dunbar syndrome is **median arcuate ligament** compression (diaphragm band throttling the coeliac trunk) striking thin young women after meals, worsening in expiration and easing in inspiration on duplex. **Celiac compression** (hooked trunk with downstream dilatation) is cured by keyhole ligament division with nerve clearance.

vis.alt: Abdominal aorta with median arcuate ligament compressing the coeliac trunk and post-stenotic dilatation.
vis.caption: Arcuate ligament hooks the coeliac trunk, worst in expiration. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: The bends of the colon are its weak points when pressure drops. After a hypotensive episode, bloody diarrhoea within two days points to the watershed zones, the Griffith point up high and the Sudeck point low down. Most cases are settled with fluids and antibiotics. Black mucosa or strictures later are managed by resection of that segment.
steps.tx: Ischaemic colitis at the watershed **Griffith point** (splenic flexure junction) and **Sudeck point** (rectosigmoid junction) presents with bloody diarrhoea within **48** hours of hypotension. Gangrene or stricture needs segmental resection, while pink mucosa with thumbprinting settles on fluids and antibiotics.
